# The Quiet Machines

The world is getting quieter, and I'm not sure we've reckoned with what that's costing us.

I don't mean the obvious din—traffic, leaf blowers, the refrigerator's hum at midnight. That's all still with us. I mean the incidental music of tools: the sounds machines made as byproducts of their work, the clatter and ding and whir that filled rooms for most of a century. They are vanishing one by one, and each takes with it a small way of knowing the world.

Consider the telephone. A rotary phone had presence. Each number you dialed came with a whir as the dial spun back to rest, and hanging up in anger produced a genuine crash, a full-body exclamation point. Today we end our angriest calls with a soft tap on glass—the least satisfying gesture in the history of human frustration. Even the ring was an actual metal bell, struck by an actual hammer, loud enough to startle a cat off a windowsill two rooms away.

Then there was the dial-up modem, whose handshake was a whole public negotiation: the hiss, the staticky squawk, the strange descending boings. That noise meant something—it was two machines arguing over speed and error correction, and a practiced ear could tell whether the argument was going well. The silence after a successful connection had a held-breath quality, like a diver slipping under.

Typewriters made work audible. An office in 1965 sounded like rain on a tin roof, dozens of small hammers striking all at once. The carriage-return bell—ding!—meant a line was finished, and the zip of the carriage sliding home was the comma between thoughts. Novels, treaties, whole administrations happened to that rhythm.

Television had its own secret frequency. Old tube sets emitted a whine at about 15.7 kilohertz that children could hear and most adults couldn't—a dog whistle for the young, an accidental hearing test administered in every living room. And stations used to sign off at night: the anthem, a test pattern, then static. Some small percentage of that static, the physicists tell us, was the afterglow of the Big Bang. For decades, falling asleep in front of the TV meant drifting off to the oldest light in the universe. Nothing on television now ever sounds like nothing.

Clocks, too, have gone mute. "Tick-tock" is not the sound of time; it's the sound of a particular mechanism, the escapement, releasing its gears one tooth at a time. The mechanism is gone and the phrase remains, a fossil noise embedded in the language—like "dialing" a number, "rolling down" a window, or "filming" on a phone. Words outlive their machines.

The street used to talk as well. Milk bottles clinked on porches at dawn. Knife grinders and rag-and-bone men sang their trades up and down the block. The ice cream truck, warbling its tune through summer neighborhoods, is among the last of these town criers—a descendant of a soundscape in which commerce announced itself out loud.

The film projector clattered at twenty-four frames per second, and the clatter was reassurance: sprockets engaged, film feeding, all well. Silence in the projection booth meant disaster. The cash register's bell announced that a transaction had been consummated. The camera's film-advance lever ratcheted the next frame into place. These weren't decorations. They were reports.

Here's the thing we didn't anticipate: we miss them, and we've started faking them. The phone camera makes a shutter click, though it has no shutter—in Japan and South Korea the click can't even be switched off. Glass keyboards tick as you type. Electric cars are fitted with manufactured engine noise, because a two-ton machine that glides up behind you in silence isn't serene; it's terrifying. We spent a century engineering noise out of our machines, then discovered we couldn't live without it, and now we synthesize the byproducts we worked so hard to eliminate.

Because those sounds were doing real work. They were ambient status reports, delivered to the ear while the eye was busy elsewhere. The modem said *connecting*. The projector said *feeding*. The clock said *passing*. A silent machine announces nothing; you have to look at it. We shifted the burden of awareness from ears to eyes, and maybe that's one reason screens feel so rapacious now—everything must be looked at to be known.

Meanwhile the losses continue, unremarked. The ringtone is dying, killed by the universal mute—an entire genre of self-expression, the carefully chosen song, gone within a decade. The startup chime has been retired and resurrected and retired again. "You've got mail" is a museum piece (the voice, incidentally, belonged to a man named Elwood Edwards, who recorded it in his living room). The annual thump of the phone book on the doorstep—gone. Even keyboard clatter thins as we migrate to glass. Every era believes its sounds are permanent. None are.

Some people saw this coming. There are archives now—an online Museum of Endangered Sounds, sound designers who keep libraries of telephone bells and typewriter strikes so that films can keep the past audible. The sound effect outlives its source by decades, a plaster cast of a vanished animal.

Every era's soundscape is an accident. Nobody composes it; it's simply the friction of that era's machines. Ours is unusually quiet, and into the quiet we've admitted new sounds—but designed ones this time: the ping, the buzz, the badge. The old noises accompanied work. The new ones interrupt it. We engineered away the friction and kept only the nagging. The machines have gone silent, and yet they've never been better at calling us.

And in twenty years, someone will write this essay about the notification ping, because even designed sounds die. The soundscape is always a sublet, never a purchase. If you want to know what an era was really like, don't look at its photographs. Close your eyes, and listen for what isn't there anymore.

I like the idea of writing about forgotten or vanishing sounds—the sounds that used to fill daily life and have disappeared or are disappearing. The sound of a telephone dial returning to rest. The clatter of typewriter keys and the ding of the carriage return. The hiss and pop of a needle finding its groove. The modem handshake. The sound of a CRT television warming up or the high-pitched whine it emitted. The slam of a phone book on a table. The scratch of chalk. Cash register bells. The whir of film projectors. This topic is rich because:
- It's concrete and sensory
- It invites reflection on time, memory, technology, and loss without being maudlin

   - Bus tokens, subway turnstiles
   - The shutter-click of actual film cameras, the advance lever
   - Ice cream truck music (endangered but alive)
   - AM radio static between stations

2. Why these sounds disappeared: they were mostly byproducts—mechanical inefficiencies, friction, resistance. Engineering eliminated them. The silent world is a world of better tolerances, smoother motors, digital processes. Noise was a symptom of energy wasted, of things rubbing against each other.

3. What we lost: sounds as information. The modem handshake told you connection was happening. The typewriter ding told you to return the carriage.
